utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, after I've asked Mr. Registrar to call the case, I'll give you an opportunity to immediately continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kecmanovic, again I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And good morning, Professor Kecmanovic. Yesterday there was some discussion about your conversations with the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership about, among other things, Sarajevo, and an exchange with the Court and with Mr. Stewart about permissible versus impermissible acts, what you understood by that and what you were aware of. And during the course of that, you explained at page 35 of the LiveNote transcript, for the benefit of counsel and the Court, that Muslim artillery had fired into Serb areas, and vice versa, and in both cases the artillery fire was opened on densely populated areas. Now, Professor Kecmanovic, that is not a complete or accurate summary of what happened in Sarajevo or what you knew about it, is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is that Serbian forces had superior artillery and laid waste to the central and old parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that what I said earlier on wasn't the complete summary, I said -- I meant something else, something that I omitted to say, and that is that the Muslim forces opened fire also targeting their own side, on their own side. And General MacKenzie was the first international official to warn us of that -- warn people of that. Those of us who lived in town and were well-informed, such as myself, we had certain information coming in to us about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's absolutely false, and you know it, sir. General MacKenzie has been at great pains, both in his book and in his interviews, to make clear that he was not in a position to assert that Bosnian Muslim forces were responsible for such atrocities. You know that.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document here, but I was in Sarajevo -- I was still in Sarajevo when General MacKenzie gave a statement to that effect, and that was something that was published by the Sarajevo media. I did not read McKenzie's book, I don't know what it says in the book, but I do know that there was a statement like that. Unfortunately, I don't have the papers here to prove that here and now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's not very difficult to go on the internet or to check General McKenzie's book and see that he says "absolutely not" in respect to allegations that he knows that Bosnian Muslim forces were responsible for such things as the bread line massacre, and you must know that.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've just said I continue to maintain; that a statement to that effect does exist and an indirect additional proof of that is this: Is that there were very heated reactions of the official forums on the Muslim side after that statement of his, and the consequence of that was that General MacKenzie has remained until the present day someone who is not liked in Muslim Sarajevo, precisely because of that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I just intervene for one second. It seems that in questions and answers, some matters are confused. I think yesterday Mr. Kecmanovic told us that densely populated areas were victimised by artillery fire and that that happened at both sides. I did not have the impression yesterday, neither from questions nor from answers, that this was a report by this witness of the balance of whether there was a superiority in terms of available artillery to one or the other party but just what people in town experienced. So therefore, these seem to be two items. I mean, even with small artillery capacity, you could target civilians, just as you could with a lot of artillery, you could refrain from targeting civilians, or at least hitting civilians. I should not speak about targeting. So these are two different matters. Then, it now -- a third matter comes in, and that is whether with a lot or just little artillery, whether there is reason to believe that the Muslims or the Serbs, whether they would hit or target those who are in their own controlled territory. These are three distinct items, and I invite you to clearly separate them in the questioning because otherwise it leads to a lot of confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I think that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, please, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, or Mr. President, may I be allowed to say something with respect to your interpretation of what I said yesterday. I didn't mention that either the Muslim forces or the Serb forces targeted civilian targets. All I said was that, as we're talking about densely populated areas, that there was -- what can I use as a term? I'm going to use a term that was used later on, after the NATO bombing of Serbia, what is called collateral damage. So the objective and target was military, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I think that exactly for that reason I withdrew the word "targeting" just a couple of lines ago and I said hitting, which means it could be collateral. I do not express myself on whether it was target or not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but at least I left that open by correcting myself. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor, during the course of answering questions this morning, I think you have begun to provide some additional insight into the information you want to provide the Court about what happened to Sarajevo. So is it essentially your position, then, that is, you want the Court to understand that there was essentially equal exchange of fire by Serbian and Muslim forces on portions of the city held by the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you one thing which I omitted to mention. You're asking me directly now. Now, I gave this addition in response to your question. You asked whether all that was the way it was, and then I made this additional explanation, not on my own initiative. I remember full well the beginning of the war --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, excuse me for a second. I'm -- if you're in the process of answering the question by referring back to the beginning of the war, I'm sure the Court will want to hear it. Otherwise, I want you first to answer my question with a yes or no. If it requires additional explanation, then you can proceed to do so. But to deflect my question by moving on to a related subject that you're more interested in talking about is not what I'm seeking. My question was: Is it essentially your position, that is, do you want the Court to understand that there was essentially equal exchange of fire by Serbian and Muslim forces on portions of the city held by the opposite side? Yes or no, and then you can explain if necessary.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer, and that is why I wanted to explain what it was about in a few words. The civilians, as I was myself, you know, at the time when there was fire, when we heard detonations, explosions, we would withdraw to the houses and we just heard the explosions. We didn't have an opportunity of seeing where, what was falling and where it was coming from. So the great problem with the civilians, with the population, was that we couldn't differentiate between what we called and what the soldiers called the ascending and descending detonations. For a layman, an explosion, a detonation sounds the same, whatever the type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, it seems that you want to tell us that you don't know. And you explained that by saying you as civilians were not in a position to get an accurate impression or accurate -- accurate impression on what actually happened in that respect. And I think that's exactly the answer, but perhaps then in the beginning you start explaining your answer, but your answer first of all is: I couldn't tell you. So if you would first start with the core of your answer and then we'll see how much more explanation is needed. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct or incorrect, Professor Kecmanovic, that Serbs had superior artillery and laid waste to central and old part of the city?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you something in continuation of my previous response, which will be closer to what you want to hear now. The consequences, the results of the shelling on the Serb side, is something that I could see, whereas the results and consequences of the effects of the Muslim forces on Serb targets I was not able to see. So my impression was, of course, that the Serb side was superior because I saw the results of their firing. What the Muslim results were as a result of the Muslim artillery fire is something that I didn't have an opportunity to see. So I think that that perhaps answers your question as you are expecting to hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not precisely, sir. I'd like to know, based on what you saw at the time, based on what you heard at the time, based on your discussions with all officials with whom you came in contact, based on everything you learned afterwards, didn't you come to the conclusion that the Serbian side had superior weaponry, superior artillery, and with that laid waste to the central and old part of the city? And why can't you just tell the Court that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I wanted to tell you. I saw the results of it, that is to say the results of that. I didn't see the results of the Muslim forces shooting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for the following reason: Mr. Tieger, you put two questions in one, and you are asking about the superiority that I understand to be whether they had better and more artillery, and you connected that question immediately that they used that to -- to damage the centre of the town. Now, you, Mr. Kecmanovic, you take the second part of the question and forget about the first part. The first question was: Are you aware, from what you heard, from what you may have seen - perhaps you have not seen it; please then tell us - whether the Serbs were superior in the artillery that was available to them compared to what the Muslims had? So that's the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite obviously I erroneously thought that I had precisely answered that question. All I saw was the power of the Serb artillery. The power of the Muslim side I was not able to control because I didn't see the results of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You limit yourself to your own observation as to how this artillery was used. Well, the question was wider. The question was: From what you heard, from what you learned, did you gain an opinion that the Serbs were by far superior in the artillery available? I'm not even at this moment thinking about use of it; that's the second part. I mean, in terms of how many pieces of artillery available. Did you learn anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as that goes, if that is a concrete question, the number of artillery and the type of artillery and so on and so forth, I didn't even have any insight into that. Although I was a member of the state Presidency, I had no insight into the side I was on, let alone the other side. I had absolutely no insight into the other side. All I could judge by was on the effects of it, so it is difficult for me to compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- as Mr. Tieger asked you, did you learn later on anything about it, about the balance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, when I moved to Belgrade, if that's what you mean, that period, once I'd left Sarajevo, then I read very different information. And that whole period until the present day, I am informing myself in a parallel fashion from more sources; Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Belgrade information and so on. And I have to say that it is very difficult to arrive at any precise data and information, and as time passed the information coming in was quite contradictory, depending on the source it came from. As to international sources, perhaps the situation would be clearer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Tieger suggests that the Serbs were superior in that respect. If you have any clear publication, since you said you informed yourself on both sides, if you have any reports - serious reports, not electoral speeches - about an artillery superiority by the Muslims at that time of the conflict in Sarajevo, then I take it that Mr. Tieger would like to see it so he can look at it. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. And let's try to get questions and answers very clear. I'll intervene when necessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to your -- may I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would like not to make it a debate but rather give an opportunity now to Mr. Tieger to put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I might be allowed just to say, as an illustration of the unclear situation, from the Sarajevo sources, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do understand that if at the end of your testimony there are matters of which you say: I really would like to say this and this and this in addition to what I said already, I will give you an opportunity. But it's not a debate; you're examined as a witness. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, this is not the first time that you've appeared before the Tribunal, nor the first time that you've provided information to the Tribunal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you provided expert reports in both the Kovacka and the Simic cases, and you testified in the Simic case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right -- no. I did not testify. So far I've appeared just as an expert witness on several occasions, but sometimes I just gave written material, handed in written material, and I wasn't called into the courtroom. I think I was called to testify just once, and I had a chance of defending - if I can use that word - my expertise, but this is the first time that I'm actually just a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic -- Mr. Tieger, is that what you meant to say in your question? Because you made a clear distinction. You talked about appearance in court only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely, Your Honour. Two reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, if you would have carefully listened to the question put to you by Mr. Tieger, he said that you provided reports in two cases and that you testified in one of them. So explaining to us that you were in court only once was not necessary because it was already included in Mr. Tieger's question, unless it was badly translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpretation wasn't correct, but I said that I testified -- it was said that I testified, it seems. I did not testify; I orally defended or presented my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll repeat the question in exactly -- there's no need to answer it anymore, but the question literally was: "So you provided expert reports in both the Kovacka and Simic cases and you testified in the Simic case." That was the question, so a simple "yes." But if there's any translation problem, it takes more time to find out. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both cases --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no. My answer is no. I was not a witness; I was an expert. I did not testify. I presented my expertise, my expert findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- but that's -- a technical linguistical matter, that is called testimony. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both cases were -- involved local, that is municipal, figures, not republic-level figures or republic-level leaders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your report in the Simic case, which you can find at tab 3 -- excuse me, in the Kvocka case, which you can find at tab 3, you said at page 29 of the English and page 48 of the B/C/S, at the very bottom and page 49 at the top: "The superior Serbian artillery laid waste to the central and old part of the city," meaning the city of Sarajevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat where I can find that portion, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom of page 48 and the top of page 49.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, is it also correct that Serbian forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a quotation from the text? Are you quoting again? And if so, would you tell me where you're quoting from. Is that a quote?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need to know whether you said it before in order to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to, but I would find my way better if I knew it because I wrote this a few years ago, you know, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Tieger first asked you whether a certain description is correct or not. Think about it, tell us whether you consider it correct or not. If this happened before, you say it's not correct, then Mr. Tieger might confront you with text you've written yourself. But we are not here to hear you verify whether you'd still agree with your report at that time, but we'd like to hear your testimony. And here you're not an expert; you're a witness. Please proceed. So tell us, please, whether it is correct that the Serbian forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this: That is precisely why I insisted on the difference between testimony and expert testimony, if that's the English word. I did not speak under oath, under the declaration, when I presented my expert findings. I did so as an expert. Now, in my role as witness, I am very careful of saying anything that I cannot back up and confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, give us -- perhaps Mr. Tieger would then ask you: Do you have any reasons to believe that the -- and then you could tell us what your sources are. I do understand that you make, rightly so, a distinction between your own observation and what you learned from other sources. Perhaps first, I do understand your answer to be that from your own observations you couldn't tell us, referring to your earlier answer; but now then perhaps include other sources for an answer to whether this statement is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking under oath here, and I'm very wary of just giving out impressions. So when the Prosecution asked me which side was stronger, I cannot claim that either side was either stronger or weaker. To say that under oath carries a lot of weight and I don't have that level of information and knowledge for me to be able to say decidedly that it was one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we are now talking about the next subject. We have verified that. As an expert you took a certain position, whereas you say that I couldn't tell you under oath that it's correct. The next one was whether it was correct that the Serbian forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills. Is that a correct statement? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say is this: It was my impression, the impression of a man who at that time lived in Sarajevo, however, not something that I can state under oath as being correct here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, I have indicated previously, and in the course of the questions you received from both Mr. Stewart and the Court I believe it was made clear, that sometimes you were being asked for a very specific event and your specific recollection of that event, sometimes you were being asked for your impressions, and sometimes you were being asked for what you knew based on what you saw, heard, learned about in conversations, or were otherwise able to glean from your activities and experiences prior to, during, and after the conflict. So I'm asking you what you knew based on -- what Nenad Kecmanovic knew based on his discussions and listening to the media and talking to leaders on both sides and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an illustration of my problems, the problems I'm facing in answering your questions, for example, the second part of this sentence about the increasing arming of the Muslims, which grew stronger with time, as it says, I knew no facts; what type of arms, the quantity of arms coming into the Muslim side. All I had was the impression that there was some movement along those lines, that they were getting stronger in their arming. I can tell you nothing more than that. It's a bit paradoxical that a man who was at the head of the army, formally speaking, the Supreme Commander, regardless of the fact that it was a collective head of state, but I do not have that information, those facts and figures, something that I could tell you here under oath as being absolutely correct. All I can give you is my impressions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to give your impressions and then we might ask on what your impressions are based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, it's not complicated. You offered some testimony about what happened in Sarajevo. It's a matter of human experience that your understanding of what happened there is going to be informed by a variety of factors. Because of your testimony previously, I asked you to clarify that understanding. That's what we've been talking about all morning and that's what I'm asking you about now. Now, as I indicated before, I had the impression from your previous testimony that you wanted the Court to understand that there was essentially an equal exchange of fire by both sides, and I'm challenging that and saying that you knew better and that conveying to the Court an accurate picture of what you understand happened in Sarajevo and what in fact happened in Sarajevo includes more than that.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not challenging your assertions that the Serb artillery was superior compared to the Muslim -- or rather, the artillery of the BH army. If that's how you understood me, then you understood me incorrectly. I'm not challenging that at all. But I myself cannot claim exactly under oath that it was indeed superior because I have no insight into the quantity of weapons, the type of weapons it had at its disposal or either side had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, no one expects you to come up with the statistics. Your own observation of the presence of artillery -- if Mr. Tieger puts to you whether it would be correct that the Serbian artillery was superior, from your last answer, instead of discussing it over 15 minutes, you could just have said: That was my impression, as well I have no reason to contest that. And then we know from this type of answer that you did not inspect every single piece of artillery, that you did not inspect the books on who bought the artillery, whether it was still there, et cetera. Let's proceed on the basis, as Mr. Tieger said, that he asked you whether that impression is right or wrong. And let's not make it a semantic game; let's make it real testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I can give you an answer, precise answer, the kind of answer you wanted to hear, if we're staying at the level of impressions, regardless of the fact that I'm a witness here under oath and not an analyst at this point, and my answer is this, my answer is this: It was my impression - just a minute, pay attention - as I said here, that it was superior, as it says, because, you see, I was on the side that could see only the results of the effects of that artillery, you know. I was in such surroundings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again you limit your answer to your own observation whereas the question was broader, was wider. Mr. Tieger, you may put the questions and I'll keep a close eye on it that it does not come a debate but rather a testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct and haven't you said previously that Serbian forces randomly showered Sarajevo with shells from the surrounding hills? Back to that question.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about out-voting and majority votes during the course of your earlier testimony to this Court and explained that, I think, as the use of numerical superiority by the Muslims and Serbs in the political context. Isn't it correct, Professor, that in your view while the Muslims and Croats did not shrink from using their numerical superiority in a political context, that the Serbian side did not shrink from using its advantage in heavy weapons in wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the result that by August it could be said that the Serbian Republic was a territorially defined entity with a population ethnically homogenised by force?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but what is your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the -- that by August of 1992 the Serbian Republic was a territorially defined entity with a population ethnically homogenised by force.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So your question is whether that's correct, or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that I quite obviously -- and we're quite obviously dealing with the text that I wrote, I seem to feel that you're quoting from something I wrote. First of all, that wasn't on the basis of direct experience because it was a period of time already when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I have to be quite clear to you. Whether Mr. Tieger is quoting or not quoting and why you did write something, et cetera, et cetera, first answer his question. His question is whether it was correct that by August of 1992 the Serbian Republic was a territorially defined entity with a population ethnically homogenised by force. That's his question. Now you tell us whether that is a correct statement, yes or no; and don't dwell on whether you ever wrote about it before. First answer questions; do not enter into a debate because it will devaluate your testimony. Please proceed. Please give an answer to that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could confirm that except for that last portion, where it says that that was done by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you want me to show you an interview where you said precisely that? Why don't you turn to tab 14, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, did you want to exhibit the report, the expert report, by Mr. Kecmanovic? And second question: In its entirety under tab 3, because that would need a number. But perhaps not the whole of the report would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, of course not the whole of the report, Your Honour, just the portion or portions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the parties would agree that on certain lines you spoke were quotes from that report. If the parties could agree on that, we could even do without the whole of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. And when Mr. Josse may be going to take an opportunity to confirm that those are accurate quotes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am not agreeable to that at all, Your Honour. In fact, I have made a note that I want discuss with Mr. Krajisnik at the next break what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then we provisionally will assign a number to tab 3, which would then be, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next tab is tab 14, and that will be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, I think the witness, as I am, is waiting for a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Just one moment, please. And my apologies. I should have referred the witness to tab 16, and the Court to tab 16. And I'm referring to the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's -- the number 1150 would be assigned to tab 16, also an interview, but now 25th of August rather than the 28th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there, Professor Kecmanovic, in tab 16, we see an interview with Belgrade Tanjug on April -- August 25th, 1992, which states in part: "The Muslim 'Bosnia,' the Croatian 'Herceg-Bosnia' and the Serbian Republic are territorially defined entities with a population ethnically homogenised by force."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you guide us to where exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the fourth paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The fourth, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, did you say that to Belgrade Tanjug, as indicated in this article, and was that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, I can confirm that as a whole, as an entity. But that was stated a little differently, differently than I understood you to have read it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor, what I want to know is whether you conveyed to Belgrade Tanjug at that time essentially that in -- focussing on the --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- focussing on the Serbian Republic for the moment, that non-Serbs were being forcibly displaced; that is, expelled from their homes by force. Isn't that what you were conveying there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to repeat what you just said; I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you conveying to Belgrade Tanjug in August 1992 that within the territories claimed by the -- and controlled by the Serbian Republic, that non-Serbs were being forcibly expelled?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I wanted to say is precisely what it says here in those four lines, which is slightly more complex, a slightly more complex formulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness should explain, Mr. Tieger. Please explain that also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to read out those four lines? "The Muslim 'Bosnia,' the Croatian 'Herceg-Bosnia' and the Serbian Republic are territorially defined entities with a population ethnically homogenised by force. After several months of the horrors of civil war, filled with hatred and fear, it seems that their sole wish is to be separated, at least temporarily ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, weren't you referring to essentially a conquest by -- again, referring specifically to the Serbian Republic in this case, by Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about both the Serbian side, the Bosnian side, and the Croatian side, and the conquests of those three sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that the conquest by the Serbian side resulted in the greatest human suffering and the greatest material destruction?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I might just be allowed to explain. May I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the extent to which on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and this is something that is shown by later reports and I'm going on to impressions once again because you've encouraged me to be able to give my impressions regardless of the fact that I'm under oath, that I can speak more freely in giving certain assessments and estimations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, would you refrain from commenting on how Mr. Tieger behaves. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I'm not trying to cut you off from explaining to the extent necessary your affirmative response to my question about the conquest by the Serbian side resulting in the greatest human suffering and the greatest material destruction, but if you want to leave it at that, I'll simply note that -- or ask you to confirm that that is precisely what you said in your report in the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, when I told you not to comment on Mr. Tieger's behaviour, I did not intend at that moment to stop you to explain what you wanted to explain, but to do that without commenting on Mr. Tieger. Just give your explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so we have a reasonably accurate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're right. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I invited Mr. Kecmanovic to give the explanation he announced he would give to us. Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry if I'm causing any trouble, if I'm making your job more difficult, but I'm simply not used to giving such brief and concise answers. It is by no means my intention to cause any difficulties, and I apologise for that. So if we established previously that the Serb army was superior, then it is only logical to conclude that they were engaged in the majority of operations in the field with respect to the material damage. It is only logical to assume that those who are superior militarily will cause more damage in the field. That is what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I can't follow your logic. Mr. Tieger, please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to clarify what was meant by "conquest," in the Kvocka report you provided an example of such conquests; in that case, the example of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you explained that in Prijedor and Sanski Most, the Serbs under the leadership of the Crisis Staffs first took power -- excuse me, under the leadership of the SDS Crisis Staffs first took power. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure of that because portion of my expert report for that case relating to local circumstances is something that I had to consult about with people who -- local people, and it is on the basis of that information that I drafted that portion of my report. So it would really help me if you could just refresh my memory by quoting the relevant passages of that report, if it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not a problem at all, sir. And for your benefit, I can tell you it's located at page -- it can be found at page 4 of the back portion of the Kvocka report, which was at tab 3, I believe. But let me quote it for you and then you can check if it doesn't ring a bell. So as I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, he needs to find it. He insists throughout his examination that he wants to find the place before he's required to answer a question like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, actually, the -- I don't -- I have no objection to that, but the witness said it would help if you could refresh my memory by quoting the relevant passages, which I was about to do, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger didn't see the witness immediately looked at the usher and was clearly beckoning for some help to find the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's no question about that in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, could you help the Chamber. Tab 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 3, page 5 of the back portion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go through it quickly, Mr. Kecmanovic, once you find it because you -- you'll have it in front of you. Look to the very back of the tab. You see the last page is numbered 5 in your version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem. Resolve, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I said, Professor, I'll go through it quickly because you can follow it there. "In Prijedor and Sanski Most there was a bloodless revolution in which the Serbs, under the leadership of the SDS Crisis Staffs, took power." Then go on to explain that there was an incident in which two Serbian policemen were killed. Then it states: "This triggered terrible --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we still have some difficulties to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 5, Your Honour, about six or seven lines down. It begins, "In Prijedor and Sanski Most ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still -- we still have not found that. Yes, we have -- in tab 3, Mr. Tieger, we have a numbering -- we have two times --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. The back portion dealing with Prijedor specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not clear on from the beginning what you understood by the back portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We found it, page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As -- I won't read that first sentence again, Professor. As I indicated, it goes on to relate an incident in which two Serbian policemen were killed and then says: "This triggered terrible repression by the Serbian military and police forces, ending in widespread expulsion of the Muslim population, not only from this village but also from the surrounding villages, and the torching of Muslim houses. A similar incident was used as a pretext to detain all Muslim men of military age in Kozarac and the surrounding area, burn their houses and expel their families." And in the succeeding paragraph you discuss Omarska and Keraterm, describing them in the middle portion of that paragraph as extremely inhumane and noting that war crimes were committed against individuals and groups of prisoners. Now, Professor, I understand, as you've explained, that this part of the report was a result of work you did with other experts who had more information than you did about what happened at the local level. The reason I brought it to your attention was to confirm that this was among the conquests that you referred to in the earlier part of the report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor, I'd like to, in light of the time, move on to a couple of other issues. You -- and that was your discussion about the meeting at the Terme Hotel in April of 1992. And you indicated during the course of your testimony that you and Mr. Pejanovic met with Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic because you simply wanted information on the situation. I think that was found at page 22356 of the transcript. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have that in my set of documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm referring to your testimony earlier in the course of this case. So now I'm -- just to re-orient you, I'm talking about your discussion --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So focussing on -- on that meeting, I believe you indicated that you simply wanted information on the situation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that wasn't just information for information's sake or out of some idle curiosity, was it? It was because of a situation of great concern that was very serious.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. I was both curious, curious professionally. I was, after all, a leader of a political party and I was in regular contact with all relevant political parties at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the underlying purpose of the meeting, the underlying reason for the meeting, was a response to what you've described as a situation of great concern and a situation that was very serious. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And presumably the hope was to find some manner of eliminating the problem, of alleviating the situation, of somehow resolving this crisis. Right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- now, it seemed that your testimony before was that the only result of this meeting, the only thing that happened at the meeting, was that everyone agreed that the situation was very serious and everyone expressed great concern, but that nothing else of value or significance was discussed. Is that how you remember it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just one in a series of attempts that I described yesterday and the day before yesterday in my testimony which did not result in anything concrete, anything specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you remember it, nobody had any ideas about how to deal with the crisis, how to address it, how to resolve it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should repeat: It was my impression that everybody, from all sides, was willing to find a political solution to the problem, but no one seems to be able to find the right solution and the right answer to the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think we know on the basis of history that no solution was found before the conflict began. The question is whether or not specific proposals for addressing or attempting to resolve the looming conflict were discussed at this meeting, rather than simply expressions of concern and agreement that it was a very serious situation.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first meeting, the one that was mentioned during this discussion. It was the first one in the series of three meetings. And at that time the situation was not as dramatic as it would become later on during the war. But neither later, on those subsequent occasions -- although, as I indicated, it seemed at one point that the agreement was close at hand, once again it yielded no specific, concrete results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take that as an answer to my question that there were no specific proposals for addressing or attempting to resolve the conflict that you remember during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could perhaps be more specific and tell you that throughout that time the problem with respect to a re-organisation of Bosnia was present at all times. There was the problem of out-voting in the parliament which, in my opinion, was the cause of the war. Then we had the mediation of Cutileiro and several different solutions were advanced, but in terms of specific proposals at the meeting, now this is something that I couldn't possibly claim existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let me show you now a portion of a speech by Dr. Karadzic made on 12th of May, 1992, to the Bosnian Serb Assembly at its 16th Session. And I don't know what's in front of you at the moment, that is, how many pages, Mr. -- Professor Kecmanovic, but the portion I'm referring to is going to be found largely at the page identified as 00847722. And as you can see at the beginning -- at the top of that page, Dr. Karadzic talks about "... the conflict in Sarajevo, where the Serbian people do not allow a city built at the expense of all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the expense of the Serbian people ..." Then he quotes some statistics and describes the development of the city at the expense of Serbian areas and then he continues: "We are not going to allow it to be excluded from our state unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We did not want war in Sarajevo. We wanted the Serbian police to control the Serbian part of the town, to be responsible for what happened in the Serbian part of the town, and Muslims for the Muslim part, and to make the partition without any fighting, both in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Sarajevo itself. All that could have been done in a peaceful manner." Now, there, Professor, Dr. Karadzic indicates his retrospective thoughts that the partition of Sarajevo could have been accomplished without fighting, despite the -- and that is what the -- Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted, as he described in that paragraph. Did neither Dr. Karadzic nor Mr. Krajisnik mention anything like that at a meeting during which everyone was expressing such concern about the serious situation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that but, generally speaking, it's difficult for me to remember things in precise terms because this was a long time ago. And more importantly, these topics were constantly on the agenda; we talked about it all the time, various maps and partitions. Later on I was involved in the drafting of those maps on the request of Karadzic and Krajisnik. At that time I did not mention it. I did not speak of the contents of the solutions, but the topic was the partition of Sarajevo and the centre of the town, where common institutions were located, that that part of the city should be a district, an extraterritorial part. So whether something to that effect was discussed at the meeting, I don't know. It is quite possible that it wasn't, but on the other hand it was a standing issue, a burning issue, at the time. But I don't remember anything specific being mentioned at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you told us during your testimony, some weeks later in the meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Krajisnik did specifically suggest the division of Sarajevo, and you told us the actions that you took in response to that. But you remember that -- if I recall your testimony correctly, that Mr. Krajisnik was suggesting a temporary division of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did he suggest temporary division of Sarajevo -- if we could spend more time talking, I would perhaps remember details. It occurred to me just now that at one point he mentioned that this was not his wish but that there was a pressure on the part of the Serbian people because of the ongoing conflict, that something to that effect should be done, but that he personally was not in favour of that and that he considered it to be only temporary solution. And as I indicated yesterday, that he was sure that he and Mr. Izetbegovic, despite their age, would see the day when the situation would return to what it had been before. As for his suggestion, it was only advanced as a matter of principle, and then he spoke to Izetbegovic because Izetbegovic had also, in principle, agreed to this temporary solution. He let Izetbegovic offer specific solutions. So I don't know how it ended, whether I was supposed to be the one to formulate those solutions in specific terms or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's useful to look at how Mr. Krajisnik recounted the potential division of Sarajevo during an interview he conducted with the BBC. That can be found at tab 23, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which has an exhibit number already. May I take it that the previous one, the minutes you showed to the witness, was P65, tab 127? And I do understand also --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 129. But at least excerpts from the 16th Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your version, that can be found, Professor Kecmanovic, at the bottom of the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is found at the top of page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 23 did my learned friend say? This is -- I don't know if I'm looking at the wrong bundle. This is an interview with Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then it would be the following tab, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have the following tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't in my bundle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it hasn't been -- become part of the tab. It needs to be distributed as an addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it that it has been presented already --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with Witness D9, if I -- my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mid-November.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This has been exhibited, I'm fairly confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm even confident that it was with Witness D9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P853, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this point in the interview, Mr. Krajisnik - and Defence counsel will assist me if I'm wrong - was discussing that period of time immediately before or just at the time of the departure of the Serbian leadership from Pale. And he said at the portion -- at the pages I indicated: "We always had at the back of our minds the division of Sarajevo - so the Serbs to have their part and the Muslims theirs. This is no secret. We consider that Sarajevo should be split into two cities - twins. So in the best of possible scenarios those peripheral regions of Sarajevo would be Serbian, while the centre would be Muslim." Now, when Mr. Krajisnik says this is no secret that the Bosnian Serbs always had in mind the division of Sarajevo, so that one part would be Muslim and one part would be Serb, is this a secret from you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were not for the last sentence you quoted, I would -- I would have thought that the matter was actually opposite to what was discussed at the meeting with Izetbegovic. When he mentioned that suburban areas should go to Serbs and the centre of the town to Muslims, Mr. Krajisnik was actually describing the factual situation, the situation that prevailed before the war and during the communist regime, referring to those peripheral regions of Sarajevo. That was the ethnic structure, ethnic composition of Sarajevo as it had been at that time. The area of the town of Sarajevo - and I assume this was probably mentioned during the case - the area commonly referred to as Bascarsija, Muslims have always lived there. They were always the majority population there. It was only later on that I learned from some historical sources how it occurred. But it was traditionally a Muslim area. It was of course not prohibited for anyone else to buy property there - there were Serbs and Croats there as well - however, historically speaking, it is true that the area actually belonged to Serb and Jewish merchants. But as for the time I'm referring to, the area was predominantly Muslim. As for the suburb and peripheral areas, my memory is that those areas were always predominantly Serb. So it was only a matter of legitimising the situation as it was on the ground. That -- that is the explanation that I can think of. As to what individuals thought of the issue and what individual opinions were of the issue, this is not something that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, if you say "that's not what you asked me about," what did Mr. Tieger ask you? Isn't it that Mr. Tieger asked you whether it was a secret to you at the time that Mr. Krajisnik was heading for a division? Not whether that would be a logical division, whether that would be a division which would be in contradiction to the existing ethnic -- you are lecturing rather than asking -- responding -- answering questions. Please listen carefully to what Mr. -- Was it a secret at that time that Mr. Krajisnik had a division of Sarajevo in his mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to what Mr. Krajisnik had in his mind at the time, I don't know what his personal thoughts were. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you did not hesitate to explain exactly to us what Mr. Krajisnik meant when he spoke those words. If I take you to your testimony, you ... "Mr. Krajisnik was actually describing the factual situation, the situation that prevailed before," et cetera, et cetera. You're interpreting Mr. Krajisnik's words without any hesitation, unsolicited to do so. So now your answer to this question is that you do not know what was on Mr. Krajisnik's mind and whether it was a secret, yes or no. Mr. Kecmanovic, no one in this courtroom would expect that a division of Sarajevo would take the form of giving Serbs control over Muslim areas or Muslims over Serb populated areas. So this explanation of logic ... This Chamber has heard quite some evidence also on Sarajevo. So the answer to the question put to you by Mr. Tieger whether it was a secret to you, that you say it was a secret to the extent that I would not know what was in Mr. Krajisnik's mind. Yes? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, during the discussions of the Cutileiro Plan and during your review of the document at tab 9, it was clear that the ethnic division of Bosnia was squarely before the international community and between the parties weeks and weeks earlier. Right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The issue of the ethnic division, the effort to ethnically divide Bosnia and Herzegovina was the central issue of the Cutileiro discussions and was squarely before the parties and the international community weeks before the conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the record of those discussions that we looked at the other day, not to mention other evidence that this Court has heard from sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and others, was that the position of the Bosnian Serbs was that they couldn't live with Muslims. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that period of time. I can explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You're saying you subsequently became aware of it but you weren't aware of it at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never heard anybody say it during the course of your involvement in the Cutileiro discussions and you never heard any Bosnian Serb leader or Bosnian Serb representative express it before the time of the meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that individuals spoke to that effect. I cannot confirm either way, but I cannot rule out the possibility that there were individuals expressing that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you certainly knew that the Bosnian Serbs were seeking a division, an ethnic division, of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, a division of that territory into Serbian, Muslim, and Croat entities. Right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the out-voting in relation to the referendum, it was since that time that the idea was circulated as the best solution or a compromise solution that would satisfy all parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now you're telling us that Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kecmanovic, the question was about what the Bosnian Serbs were seeking. So if you would first answer that question. If you would say others did as well, fine, but please focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want it repeated, sir? My question was: You certainly knew, did you not, that the Bosnian Serbs were seeking an ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, a division of the territory into Serbian, Muslim, and Croat entities.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- but your testimony --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but may I add something? Would you allow me to add something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not entirely -- it's not clear to me why anything needs to be added, but proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a matter that was -- could not be ignored. It was a topic of all public conversations. I participated. I was part of the commission, Cutileiro commission, and that's why the question is not specific enough. I would like you to refer me to what specific -- what specifically you have in mind when you ask this question. I just want to understand better your question and for us to understand each other better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for better understanding perhaps 25 minutes of a break would help us. We'll adjourn and have a break, Mr. Kecmanovic, until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, I want to take you back to one of the last items you discussed during the course of your examination-in-chief by Mr. Stewart, and that was excerpt from the book by Misha Glenny.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it may be helpful if the witness can have that exhibit before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was a Defence exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no translation yet, Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you should be aware. Perhaps if you want to put to the witness a certain portion, perhaps you could slowly read that so that both the witness and Mr. Krajisnik can follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Kecmanovic, let me ascertain from you the extent to which it will be necessary or helpful to cite the entire excerpt that was the focus of the discussion earlier. First of all, generally I take it you remember the excerpt and the discussion with Mr. Stewart. And as I understand it, that was a reflection of a conversation that -- between you and Mr. Glenny that you couldn't recall in its entirety but recall generally certain aspects of?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to focus you on a part of the book that places it in context, the passage that Mr. Stewart quoted began: "Nenad Kecmanovic served for a short time ..." was a brief introductory passage that -- for the benefit of the reader. But immediately before that and immediately after that Mr. Glenny places the conversation in context, and let me provide that for you. So the paragraph immediately before said: "In the first phase of the war, the world media focussed most of their attention on the plight of the besieged capital, Sarajevo. There was no special reason why the Bosnian Serb leadership channeled so much of its military effort into the siege. While it was in their interests to cut communication links with the Bosnian government strongholds to the north and west, the gratuitous destruction of Sarajevo itself was merely an expression of hatred." And then -- so that's the portion that precedes the description of your conversation with Mr. Koljevic. And then -- of course, at the end of the -- the conversation that he relates ends in the following way, with Dr. Koljevic nodding his head sagely about being too personally involved with Sarajevo and then adding absent-mindedly as an afterthought: "Of course with everybody worrying about Sarajevo, it means that they don't pay much attention to what's going on elsewhere." And then Mr. Glenny continues in his book: "In early August, however, the world did begin to learn about the bestial things that had been happening in eastern and northern Bosnia." And explains that, "This was largely due to some particularly courageous reporting ..." Now, it's -- the point of that story and the point of Mr. -- of Dr. Koljevic's afterthought that no one was paying much attention to what was going on elsewhere, as indicated by Mr. Glenny, was that it deflected focus -- that the attention to Sarajevo by the international community, among others, deflected focus from what was happening in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that right, and isn't that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, as I said when Mr. Stewart was quoting this, I remember that evening and the dinner I had with Koljevic and Glenny, but I denied some concrete allegations as simply being incorrect. Now, as far as this part is concerned, I said that I don't remember that that's how it was, that I do know that I said that all of us in one way or another had been occupied with Sarajevo, and it was logical for me because I spent the whole of the war in Bosnia in Sarajevo. Now, as to the continuation, I really can't say, I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I'd note for the record that your denial of some concrete allegation as simply being incorrect, I'll remind you, was a product of either a translation misunderstanding or the fact that you didn't hear that Glenny, in his account, said that the reports that you had fled Sarajevo for your safety and arrived in a very poor condition were erroneous. You'll recall that, right? That he was saying those were erroneous; we wasn't saying that that was true. And you began to deny it and then you realised, in fact, that the two of you were in agreement. Okay. I see you nodding your head, so I'll take that as an affirmative response.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not an affirmative response. When we're talking about allegations that I was beaten up in Sarajevo, that was too personal a matter and too serious a matter for me not to have remembered that. Had I been beaten up, I would have remembered that very well to the present day. Now, when we come to certain quotes from a conversation during a dinner or in the course of an evening, that is something I am less likely to remember, and that's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you made the point yesterday that Mr. Krajisnik was fond of repeating one of his stories and told us how you jokingly used to indicate you were prepared to leave the room if he was about to embark on a similar account. And Mr. Koljevic, too, like, I suppose, all the rest of us, was also, at least occasionally, prone to repeat some stories or observations. Right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is linked to Mr. Krajisnik, they were regular sessions, parliamentary -- our parliamentary parties, their leaders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, if you say that -- let me just move on to the issue I want to bring your attention to. I'd like to present you with another conversation that Dr. Koljevic had on the same subject and see if that refreshes your recollection about this conversation that you and Dr. Koljevic had that you related to Mr. Glenny.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could have that presented to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, while doing so, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to draw your attention to when earlier you referred -- I think it was 26 or 24, I'm not quite sure. The interview, when you said to the witness, you're reported to say this and this and this. I noticed that the English version does not have quotation marks where the B/C/S version has. Now, I do not know what is the original, but someone has either left out or put quotation marks in there. Now, the witness gave his testimony on the matter, but I'm not very happy to see two versions of a -- one which seems to describe just a situation, another where it's a description of the situation is in quotation marks for the person interviewed. So could you please try to find that out. I think it was one of the Tanjug, where you started giving us the wrong one, and I think it was finally 24 or 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know which exhibit you're referring to, Your Honour, and I'll be happy to, of course, check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please try to find out. Then we go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, this is an excerpt from another journalist, in this case, Ed Vulliamy, out of a book entitled "Seasons in Hell." And he relates a conversation with Dr. Koljevic in which the same subject was discussed. And I'll read that. "At this point of the war, the worst had been hidden from eye-witnesses, and could be gleaned only after the event, from witnesses' testimony. Unlike the siege of Sarajevo, which was there for all to see, the ethnic cleansing programme was not for public consumption. Karadzic's intellectual shadow, a Serbian member of the Bosnian Presidency Nikola Koljevic, later admitted to me that Sarajevo was designated a piece of violent theatre which could captivate world attention and draw it away from the principal programme. Professor Koljevic, who has good English and pedantically quotes Shakespeare to illustrate every point, chastised me over tea and cakes in a smart Belgrade hotel: 'It amazes me that you all took so long to get to the point.'" Now I'm indicating a quote from Professor Koljevic: "It amazes me that you all took so long to get to the point. Poor Sarajevo! That was all you could think about. The crossroads of Europe! None of you had ever been on holiday in Trnopolje, Ha Ha!" Professor Kecmanovic, does that refresh your recollection about the conversation with Dr. Koljevic and the point he was making about the attention focussed on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of two things here: One thing is that I lived in Sarajevo right up until the 5th of July, 1992. That's one fact. And the second fact is that I was not a member of the Serbian National Movement or the SDS. And you, during what you said yesterday, quoted certain facts with relation to the Serbian Democratic Party and the media, Serb media towards me, and you quoted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I'm going to stop you again. You're not answering the question. The question was whether this quote from a book of Ed Vulliamy, whether that refreshes your memory, that is, that brings back into your mind, perhaps being of a similar nature, the discussion you had with Professor Koljevic. Reading this, brings that anything to you as far as your recollection of your conversation with Mr. Koljevic is concerned? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, without regard to the very specifics - and I know you're a stickler for specifics, Professor - isn't it the case that what you communicated to Mr. Glenny was that Dr. Koljevic had added as an afterthought that the benefit of all the focus on Sarajevo was that it deflected the attention of the international community to the events that were happening elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That portion - and I have to repeat - as far as I remember, that part of the conversation did not have any contents like that or that meaning, to the best of my recollections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have -- do you have any explanation for why Mr. Glenny understood you to be communicating that by your account of the conversation to him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Communicating what? My account what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the excerpts in Mr. Glenny's book, does it not seem clear to you that he understood that the focus of that comment by Dr. Koljevic and the focus of bringing it to his attention was to note that the world media had focussed its attention on Sarajevo and not its attention on what was happening elsewhere in Bosnia but that it finally began to come out in August?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sense of my intervention that Glenny mentions - and as far as I remember, that is correct that I did say that we were concentrating on Sarajevo too much - the sense of that sentence of mine was this: That in the conversation that we were having at the time, we were dealing with Sarajevo exclusively. And my intervention went along quite different lines; the sense of it was quite different. You must understand this: It wasn't a formal, official conversation of any kind. We were sitting down to dinner, Glenny, Koljevic and myself, we were having dinner, and we were having a conversation. Koljevic asked about Sarajevo a great deal, and I can repeat that part of his family -- his brother was in the city of Sarajevo, he was down there, so we were discussing things like that. And to the best of my recollections, this story, personal stories around Sarajevo, was for this third person in our conversation at the dinner was that we were too -- concentrating on Sarajevo too much, rather than the political connotation that this seems to have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Josse, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, my case manager reminded me that the previous exhibit did not get a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the newly provided --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The excerpt from the book entitled "Seasons in Hell," Your Honours, will be given the provisional Exhibit number P1151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. That's author Ed Vulliamy. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I spent most of the last break with Mr. Krajisnik. I need to spend some more time with him. He has given me a document which he would like me to ask the witness some questions about. I really need to discuss that further. I also am far from clear that it arises from cross-examination. So I may need to seek leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And you need more time for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, as much time as the Court is prepared to give me realistically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we would like to finish today, so what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you need -- then we make this half an hour the second break, which means that we would restart at 12.00, which might also limit our time for the remainder of the morning, but I think we would be able to finish at approximately 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. As Your Honour is aware, the next witness is not in this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I do -- I do understand that you want to start the examination of that witness tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
